It is entirely Meccan, according to al-Ḥasan, ʿIkrimah, ʿAṭāʾ and Jābir. Ibn ʿAbbās said: "Except for three verses, from His saying ﴿But if you are in doubt﴾ to the end of them."

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: **(Alif. Lām. Rāʾ.)** There are four interpretations of it:

First: its meaning is "I am Allah, the All-Seeing." This was said by Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Ḍaḥḥāk.

Second: they are letters from the name of Allah, which is al-Raḥmān (the Most Merciful). This was said by Saʿīd ibn Jubayr and al-Shaʿbī.

Sālim ibn ʿAbd Allāh said: "(Alif. Lām. Rāʾ.), (Ḥā. Mīm.) and (Nūn) are segments of al-Raḥmān."

Third: it is one of the names of the Qur'an. This was said by Qatādah.

Fourth: they are openings with which Allah began the Qur'an. This was said by Ibn Jurayj.

**﴿These are the verses of the Wise Book﴾**. By His saying **﴿These are the verses﴾** He means: "These are verses," as al-A'shā said:

*"Those are my horses from him, and those are my saddles; their foals are yellow like raisins."*

[p. 421] That is: "These are my horses."

Regarding **﴿the Wise Book﴾** here there are three sayings. First: the Torah and the Gospel. This was said by Mujāhid.

Second: the Psalms (al-Zabūr). This was said by Maṭar.

Third: the Qur'an. This was said by Qatādah.

Regarding His saying **﴿the Wise﴾** there are two interpretations. First: it means "muḥkam" (perfectly firm and precise). This was said by Abū ʿUbayda.

Second: it is as if it speaks with wisdom. This was mentioned by ʿAlī ibn ʿĪsā.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: **﴿Is it a wonder for the people that We have revealed to a man from among them, [saying]: "Warn the people"?﴾** Ibn ʿAbbās said: The occasion of its revelation was that when Allah, Exalted is He, sent Muḥammad (ﷺ) as a messenger, the Arabs denied that, or those among them who denied it said: "Allah is greater than that His messenger should be a human like Muḥammad." Third: that they will have a true intercessor [shafīʿ ṣidq], meaning Muḥammad (ﷺ), who will intercede for them. This was said by Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān.

And it may be a sixth: that "a sure standing" (qadam ṣidq) means that the truth of the reward matches the truth of the obedience, with "standing" being an expression for precedence and "truth" an expression for what is real.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (*al-Nukat wa al-'Uyun*) on Surah 10, verses 3–6:

His statement, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿He governs the affair﴾. There are two interpretations regarding it. The first: He decides it alone. This is the view of Mujahid.

The second: He commands it and executes it.

﴿There is no intercessor except after His permission﴾. There are three interpretations regarding it. The first: there is no intercessor who is granted intercession except after Allah, exalted is He, permits him to intercede.

The second: no one speaks in His presence except with His permission. This is the view of Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

The third: there is no second with Him. It is derived from *shaf'* (pairing), which is the couple, because He created the heavens and the earth while He is one and alone, with no living being with Him, and then He created the angels and humankind.

[p. 423] And His statement, ﴿except after His permission﴾, means: after His command that creation should come into being, so it came into being. This is the view of Ibn Bahr.

His statement, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿Indeed, He originates creation, then He repeats it﴾. There are two interpretations regarding it. The first: He brings it into being, then He annihilates it.

The second, which is the view of Mujahid: He gives it life, then makes it die, then destroys it, then gives it life again.

Al-Mawardi's commentary (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on Surah 10, verses 9–10:

God, the Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds, their Lord will guide them by their faith﴾. Regarding this there are four interpretations. The first: He will make for them a light by which they walk. This is the view of Mujahid.

The second: He will make their deeds a guide for them to Paradise. This is the meaning of the statement of Ibn Jurayj.

It has been narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "A believer's deed will meet him in its most beautiful form (p-424), so it will comfort him and guide him, and a disbeliever's deed will meet him in its most hideous form, so it will terrify him and lead him astray."

The third: that God guides them to the path of Paradise.

The fourth: that He describes them with guidance as a form of praise for them.

﴿Rivers will flow beneath them﴾. Regarding this there are two interpretations. One: beneath their dwellings. This is the view of Abu Malik.

The second: they will flow in front of them while they see them from above, based on the words of the Exalted: ﴿Does not the dominion of Egypt belong to me, and these rivers flow beneath me?﴾ [az-Zukhruf: 51], meaning, in front of me.

Abu Ubayda related from Masruq that the rivers of Paradise flow without a trench.

God, the Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿Their call therein will be: "Glory be to You, O Allah"﴾. Regarding this there are two interpretations. One: when the people of Paradise desire something or want to request something, they say, "Glory be to You, O Allah," and then that thing comes to them. This is the view of al-Rabi' and Sufyan.

The second: when they wish to turn to God in supplication, their supplication to Him is: "Glory be to You, O Allah." This is the view of Qatada.

﴿And their greeting therein will be: "Peace"﴾. Regarding this there are two interpretations. One: its meaning is that their dominion therein is secure. The word tahiyya (greeting) means dominion, and from it is the verse of Zuhayr ibn Janab al-Kalbi:

"And whatever a young man attains, I have attained it, except the tahiyya."

The second: that the greeting of some of them to others therein is "Peace," meaning: you are safe and secure from what the people of the Fire were afflicted with. This is the view of Ibn Jarir al-Tabari.

﴿And the last of their call will be: "Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds"﴾. Regarding this there are two interpretations. One: the last of their supplication is "Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds," just as the first of their supplication was "Glory be to You, O Allah." This is probably the view of Qatada.

The second (p-425): when He responds to them in what they called upon Him for and gives them what they desired when they asked with glorification, they say after it: "Thanks be to Allah, and praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds."

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 10, verse 11:

His saying, exalted and majestic is He: ﴿And if Allah were to hasten for people the evil as they seek to hasten the good, their term would have been decreed for them﴾. Concerning this there are two interpretations.

The first: And if Allah were to hasten for the disbeliever the punishment for his disbelief, as He hastened for him the good of this world in wealth and children, He would have hastened for him the fulfilment of his term, so that he would hasten the punishment of the Hereafter. This is what Ibn Ishaq said.

The second: Its meaning is that a man, when he becomes angry at himself, his property, or his child, prays for evil against it, saying: "May Allah not bless it, and may Allah destroy it." Then, if that were answered for him as good is answered for him, their term would have been decreed for them, i.e., they would have perished.

Accordingly, on the first interpretation the explanation is specific to the disbeliever, and on the second interpretation it is general, applying to both the Muslim and the disbeliever.

The second: in their misguidance, said by al-Rabi' ibn Anas.

﴿wandering blindly﴾. Concerning this there are three interpretations. The first: they hesitate, said by Ibn Abbas, Abu Malik and Abu al-'Aliyah.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (*al-Nukat wa al-'Uyun*) on Surah 10, verses 15–17:

His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He: ﴿And when Our clear verses are recited to them﴾, meaning the verses of the Qur'an, which are "an explanation of everything."

﴿Those who do not expect to meet Us say﴾, meaning the polytheists of Makkah.

﴿Bring a Qur'an other than this, or change it.﴾ The difference between changing it and bringing something other than it is that changing it cannot be done alongside it, whereas bringing something other than it may be done alongside it.

There are three aspects to their saying that:

The first: they asked him to turn promise into threat, threat into promise, the permitted into the forbidden, and the forbidden into the permitted. This was said by Ibn Jarir al-Tabari.

The second: they asked him to remove from the Qur'an the disparagement of their gods and the mockery of their intellects. This was said by Ibn 'Isa.

The third: they asked him to drop what it contains of the mention of resurrection and rising. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

﴿Say: It is not for me to change it on my own accord.﴾ That is, it is not for me to receive it with alteration and change, just as it is not for me to receive it with rejection and denial.

﴿I follow only what is revealed to me﴾ in what I recite to you of promise, threat, permitting, forbidding, command, or prohibition.

﴿Indeed, I fear, if I disobey my Lord﴾ by altering or changing it,

﴿the punishment of a tremendous Day.﴾ That is, the Day of Resurrection.

His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He: ﴿Say: Had Allah willed, I would not have recited it to you﴾, meaning the Qur'an, ﴿nor would He have made you know of it﴾. On this there are three aspects:

The first: nor would I have informed you of it. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: nor would I have warned you of it. This was said by Shahr ibn Hawshab.

The third: nor would I have made you aware of it. This was said by Qatada.

﴿For I have remained among you a lifetime before it.﴾ On this there are two aspects:

The first: he meant the span of his life before the revelation came to him, since a person's lifespan is the period of his life, whether long or short.

The second: that it was forty years, because the Prophet ﷺ was sent after forty, which is the age at which a person's life is considered complete. This was said by Qatada.

﴿Will you not then reason?﴾ That I did not leave that aside after I had remained among you a lifetime until it was revealed to me, and had I fabricated it, I would have put it forward.

The first: they asked him to turn promise into threat, threat into promise, the permitted into the forbidden, and the forbidden into the permitted. This was said by Ibn Jarir al-Tabari.

The second: they asked him to remove from the Qur'an the disparagement of their gods and the mockery of their intellects. This was said by Ibn 'Isa.

﴿Indeed, I fear, if I disobey my Lord﴾ by altering or changing it,

His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He: ﴿Say: Had Allah willed, I would not have recited it to you﴾, meaning the Qur'an, ﴿nor would He have made you know of it﴾. On this there are three aspects:

The first: nor would I have informed you of it. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: nor would I have warned you of it. This was said by Shahr ibn Hawshab.

The third: nor would I have made you aware of it. This was said by Qatada.

The first: he meant the span of his life before the revelation came to him, since a person's lifespan is the period of his life, whether long or short.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 10, verses 20–23:

His words, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And when We let the people taste mercy after adversity had touched them﴾. Regarding this, there are four interpretations:

First: ease after hardship.

Second: well-being after sickness.

Third: abundance after drought. This is the view of al-Dahhak.

Fourth: Islam after disbelief, which is the hypocrite. This was said by al-Hasan.

(p-430) ﴿When they have a plot against Our signs﴾. Regarding this, there are two interpretations:

One: that the plot here is disbelief and denial. This was said by Ibn Bahr.

The second: that it is mockery and denial. This was said by Mujahid.

It may also carry a third meaning: that the plot here is hypocrisy, because the hypocrite displays faith and conceals disbelief.

﴿Say: Allah is swifter in plotting﴾, meaning: swifter in requiting the plot.

It has also been said that the occasion of its revelation was that when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) invoked a drought upon the people of Makkah, and they suffered famine for seven years like the years of Yusuf, in response to his supplication, Abu Sufyan came to him and said: "O Muhammad, you have indeed invoked drought and we have been stricken with drought. So call upon Allah for us for abundance; if He answers you and we are blessed with abundance, we will believe you and have faith in you." So he prayed for them and sought rain, and they were given rain and were blessed with abundance. Then they broke what they had said and persisted in their disbelief. This is the meaning of His words: ﴿When they have a plot against Our signs﴾.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So We made them a harvest﴾. Regarding this there are two views. The first: *dhāhiban* (gone, perished). The second: *yābisan* (dried up).

﴿As if they had not flourished yesterday﴾. Regarding this there are four interpretations. The first: "as if they had not been inhabited yesterday," related by al-Kalbi. The second: "as if they had not lived yesterday," related by Qatadah, and from this is the verse of Labid:

*"She enjoyed a week after the course of Dahis, were there an immortality for the stubborn soul."*

The third: "as if they had not stood (in it) yesterday." From the phrase of the Arabs, "So-and-so enjoyed the place (*ghaniya bi-l-makān*)" when he stayed in it. This was related by Ali ibn Isa. The fourth: "as if they had not been in comfort yesterday," also related by Qatadah.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And God calls to the Abode of Peace﴾, meaning Paradise.

Regarding its being named the Abode of Peace there are two views. The first: because *al-Salām* is God Himself, and Paradise is His abode. The second: because it is the abode of safety from every calamity, related by al-Zajjaj.

﴿And He guides whom He wills to a straight path﴾. Regarding His guidance there are two views. The first: by granting success and assistance. The second: by manifesting proofs and establishing evidences.

Regarding "the straight path" there are four interpretations. The first: that it is the Book of God, the Exalted. Ali ibn Abi Talib related, saying: I heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say: "The straight path is the Book of God, the Exalted."

The second: that it is Islam, related by al-Nawwas ibn Sam'an from the Messenger of God (ﷺ).

The third: that it is the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and his two companions after him, Abu Bakr and Umar, said by al-Hasan and Abu al-Aliyah.

The fourth: that it is the Truth, said by Mujahid and Qatadah.

Jabir ibn Abd Allah related: "The Messenger of God came out to us one day and said: 'I saw in a dream as if Jibril was at my head and Mika'il was at my feet. Your likeness and the likeness of your community is that of a king who built a house, then built within it a dwelling, then set in it a table, then sent a messenger calling the people to his food. Whoever answers you enters Islam, whoever enters Islam enters Paradise, and whoever enters Paradise eats of what is in it.'" Then Qatadah and Mujahid recited:

﴿And God calls to the Abode of Peace﴾

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 10, verse 26–27:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿For those who have done good﴾ means worshipping their Lord.

﴿The best (al-husna) and more⦗ziyadah⦘﴾. Concerning this there are five interpretations:

The first: al-husna is Paradise, and the ziyadah (increase) is looking upon the Face of Allah, exalted is He. This is the saying of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman, and Abu Musa al-Ash'ari.

The second: al-husna is one of the good deeds, and the ziyadah is its multiplication up to ten times its like. This was said by Ibn Abbas.

The third: al-husna is one good deed like another good deed, and the ziyadah is forgiveness and good pleasure (ridwan). This was said by Mujahid.

The fourth: al-husna is the recompense in the Hereafter, and the ziyadah is what they were given in this world. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

The fifth: al-husna is the reward, and the ziyadah is its permanence. This was said by Ibn Bahr.

It may also admit a sixth: al-husna is what they wish for, and the ziyadah is what they desire.

﴿And no darkness (qatar) shall cover their faces﴾. Regarding the word yarhaqu (cover/overtake) there are two meanings: the first: it rises over (ya'lu). The second: it reaches (yalhaqu); from this it is said "ghulam muraahiq" (a youth who has reached the men) when he joins the men.

Regarding His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿qatar﴾ there are four meanings: the first: it is the blackness of the faces, said by Ibn Abbas. The second: it is sorrow, said by Mujahid. The third: it is smoke, from which comes qutar al-lahm (the smell of roasting meat) and qutar al-'ud (the smoke of aloes-wood), said by Ibn Bahr. The fourth: it is the dust in their gathering toward Allah, exalted is He, and from it is the saying of the poet:

"Crowned with the mantle of kingship, followed by a wave, above which you see the banners and the dust (qatar)."

﴿Nor humiliation (dhillah)﴾. Here there are two meanings: the first: disgrace (al-hawan). The second: failure (al-khaybah).

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 10, verse 28–33:

His saying, exalted and majestic is He: ﴿There every soul will know what it has sent before﴾. In this there are two readings. The first: with two tā' (tabluwā, "will experience/undergo"), which Ḥamzah and al-Kisā'ī recited. There are three interpretations of it:

First: every soul will follow what it sent ahead in the world (tatba'u, "follow"). This is related from al-Suddī, and from it is the saying of the poet:

"Indeed the doubter follows the doubter, just as you see the wolf following the wolf."

Second: every soul will read (tatlū, "recite") the book of its good deeds and the book of its bad deeds, and this is from recitation (al-tilāwah).

Third: every soul will witness (tu'āyinu, "see directly") the recompense for what it did.

The second reading, which is the reading of the rest (of the Readers), is tatlū with a bā' (tabluwā, "test/try"). In its interpretation there are two aspects:

One of them: every soul will be tested (tusallimu, "will be made to submit/hand over").

The second: every soul will be examined (takhtabiru), as related by Mujāhid.

﴿And they will be returned to God, their true Master (mawlāhum al-ḥaqq)﴾. That is, their Owner. He, exalted is He, described Himself as "the Truth" (al-Ḥaqq) because the truth is from Him, just as He described Himself as "the Just" ('adl), because justice is from Him.

If it is said: He, exalted is He, has said: ﴿and that the disbelievers have no protector (mawlā) for them﴾ [Muhammad: 11]. How then is there a protector (mawlā) for them here? It is said: He is not a protector in the sense of support and aid; He is a mawlā for them in the sense of ownership (al-milkiyyah).

﴿And what they used to fabricate will vanish from them﴾. That is, what they used to lie about will be nullified for them.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 10, verses 37–40:

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And this Qur'an could not have been produced by other than Allah﴾ means that it could not be fabricated and falsely attributed (to Allah).

﴿But it is a confirmation of what was before it﴾ has two interpretations. The first: it is a witness to the truth of what preceded it of the Torah, the Gospel and the Psalms (al-Zabur).

The second: it confirms what lies before it of resurrection (al-Ba'th), rising (al-Nushur), recompense (al-Jaza') and reckoning (al-Hisab).

It may also bear a third meaning: that its meaning is "But those earlier Books that are before it will confirm it, through what they contain of mention of it, and thus the fabrication will be removed from it."

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Rather, they denied that which they did not encompass in knowledge of it﴾ has two interpretations. (p-436) The first: they did not know what would befall them through their denial, because of their doubt about it.

The second: they did not encompass knowledge of what it contains of promise and warning, due to their turning away from it.

﴿And its interpretation (ta'wil) has not yet come to them﴾ has two interpretations. The first: knowledge of the proof (al-Burhan) contained in it.

The second: what their affair will lead to of punishment (al-'Iqab).

(p-437) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And the Day He gathers them, it will be as if they had not remained [in the world] except an hour of the day﴾. In this there are two interpretations:

al-Kalbi said: they will recognize one another when they come out of their graves, and then the recognition will be cut off.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 10, verse 50–56:

The Exalted's saying: ﴿And they ask you (wa-yastanbi'unaka)﴾, meaning they ask you for information (yastakhbirunaka), and it is a seeking of news (talab al-naba').

﴿Is it true?﴾ (ahaqqun huwa) has two interpretations. The first: it refers to the Resurrection (al-ba'th), as said by al-Kalbi.

The second: it refers to the punishment in the Hereafter (al-'adhab fi al-akhirah).

﴿Say: Yes, by my Lord, it is indeed true﴾ (qul iy wa-rabbi innahu la-haqq). He swore an oath together with informing them that it is true, for emphasis (ta'kidan).

﴿And you cannot escape﴾ (wa-ma antum bi-mu'jizin). It has two interpretations. The first: you cannot be prevented (bi-mumtani'in). The second: you cannot outrun (bi-sabiqin), as said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The Exalted's saying: ﴿And they will conceal their regret (wa-asarru al-nadamah) when they see the punishment﴾. It has two interpretations. The first: they concealed their regret and hid it from their leaders. It is also said that rather, the leaders concealed it from their followers.

The second: they displayed it and made it manifest to them.

Al-Mubarrad mentioned a third interpretation: that the regret appeared in the "asirrat" (folds, or the sunken lines) of their faces, which are the creases of the forehead (takasir al-jabhah).

﴿And it will be judged between them﴾ (wa-qudiya baynahum). It has two interpretations. The first: it was judged between them and their leaders, as said by al-Kalbi.

The second: He decreed against them what they deserve of their punishment.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 10, verses 71–73:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So resolve upon your plan, and [gather] your partners﴾. In this there are two views. The first: "Gather your plan and call upon your partners to help you," said by al-Farra'. The second: "Gather your plan together with your partners in mutual support," said by al-Zajjaj.

Regarding this "gathering" (ijma', here meaning unifying the resolve) there are two views. The first: that it means preparation. The second: that it means determination.

﴿Then let not your plan be concealed from you⁠ ⁠⁠⁠— ⁠⁠⁠⁠(ghumma)⁠ ⁠⁠. In this there are two interpretations. The first: that ghumma is the constriction of the matter that causes distress. The second: that it is the covered, from their saying: "The moon was ghumma" when it was concealed.

Regarding what is meant by "the matter" here, there are two views. The first: those whom they call upon besides Allah, may He be exalted. The second: the resolve they hold.

﴿Then carry out your decision against me⁠ ⁠⁠— ⁠ ⁠⁠ (iqdu ilayya)⁠ ⁠⁠. In this there are three views. The first: "Then rise up," said by Ibn 'Abbas. The second: "Then carry out against me whatever you are going to carry out," said by Qatada. The third: "Carry out against me what is in your souls," said by Mujahid.

﴿And give me no respite﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: "Do not delay me."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿But if you turn away﴾, meaning from faith.

﴿Then I have not asked you for any reward﴾. This may bear two meanings. The first: "I have not asked you for any reward that you find burdensome, so that you refrain from responding because of it, ﴿my reward is only from Allah﴾." The second: "I have not asked you for any reward, for if it were cut off from me it would weigh heavily upon me."

﴿My reward is only from Allah﴾, and it has been attained through the supplication for you, whether you respond or refuse.

﴿And I have been commanded to be among the Muslims﴾, that is, among those who submit to the command of Allah by obeying Him.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So We saved him and those with him in the ship﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: In the ship of Noah, peace be upon him, there were eighty men, one of whom was Jirhum, whose tongue was Arabic. He carried in it two of every pair. Ibn 'Abbas said: the first thing he carried was the ant, and the last thing he carried was the dung beetle, and Iblis entered with him, clinging to his tail.

﴿And We made them successors﴾, that is, successors to those who perished by drowning.

﴿And We drowned those who denied Our signs﴾. Abu Zuhayr related that the people of Noah lived in the flood for forty days.

Muhammad ibn Ishaq mentioned that the water remained after the drowning for one hundred and fifty days, so that the period between Allah's sending of the flood and the subsiding of the water was six months and ten days, which is one hundred and ninety days.

Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: When forty nights had passed over Noah, he opened the window of the ship, then sent out the raven to see what the water had done, but it did not return. He then sent the dove, which returned to him, finding no place for its foot. Then he sent it again after seven days, and it returned to him at evening with an olive leaf in its beak, so he knew that the water had receded from the earth. Then he sent it again after seven days, and it did not return, so he knew that the earth had emerged. The ship settled upon al-Judi on the seventeenth night of the seventh month, as has been related, and Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 10, verses 74–78:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿They said: "Have you come to us to turn us away (lataftana) from what we found our fathers upon?"﴾ Concerning this there are three opinions:

First: "to twist us" (litalwina, i.e., to distort or divert us), as said by Qatadah.

Second: "to hinder us" (litasuddana), as said by al-Suddi.

Third: "to turn us aside" (litasrifana), from their saying: "lafatahu laftan," meaning he turned it aside, and from it: "lafata ʿunuqahu," meaning he twisted his neck (lawaha). This was said by ʿAli ibn ʿIsa.

﴿And that greatness (al-kibriya') may be yours in the land﴾ Concerning this there are four opinions: (p-445) First: kingship (al-mulk), as said by Mujahid.

Second: magnificence (al-ʿazamah), related by al-Aʿmash.

Third: height or superiority (al-ʿuluww), as said by ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam.

Fourth: obedience (al-taʿah), as said by al-Dahhak.

**Al-Mawardi's commentary (al-Nukat wa al-'Uyun) on Surah 10, verses 84–86:**

His words, Exalted and Majestic is He: ﴿Upon Allah do we rely﴾ admit of two interpretations. The first: [it means] in submission to Him. The second: [it means] in trust in Him.

The second: do not give them power over us, so that they are tempted through us, because they think they are upon the truth. This is said by Abu al-Duha and Abu Mijlaz.

His words, Exalted and Majestic is He: ﴿And We revealed to Musa and his brother: "Settle your people in Egypt in houses"﴾. He means: choose and take for them houses in which they will dwell. From this is the saying of the rajaz (a poetic metre) poet:

*Glory has settled [tabawwa'a] among us, and so has kingship.*

The second: mosques. This is said by al-Dahhak.

The second: make your mosques facing the Ka'bah. This is said by Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatadah.

The third: make your houses that are in Syria a qiblah for you in prayer; it is the qiblah of the Jews to this day. This is said by Ibn Bahr.

The fourth: make your houses face one another. This is said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

﴿And establish the prayer﴾. In it there are two interpretations: The first: in your houses, so that you are safe from Pharaoh.

The second: facing the qiblah of Makkah, so that your prayer is valid.

﴿And give good news to the believers﴾. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: give them good news of victory in this world, and of Paradise in the Hereafter.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 10, verses 90–92:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿So today We shall save you in your body﴾. The meaning of "nunajjika" (We shall save you) is "nulqika" (We shall cast you) upon a high place (najwah) of the earth, and najwah is an elevated place. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿in your body﴾ has two interpretations. The first: meaning in your body without a soul (ruh), said by Mujahid.

The second: with your armour (bi-dir'ika), for he had an iron armour by which he was recognised. This was said by Abu Sakhr, and those among the people of Pharaoh who had stayed behind used to deny his drowning.

Yazid al-Yazidi recited "nunajjika" with an unpointed ha' (nuhajjika) and Alqamah transmitted it from Ibn Mas'ud.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 10, verse 93:

His saying, exalted and majestic is He: ﴿And We certainly settled the Children of Israel in a good settlement⦗mubawwa’ sidq⦘﴾. Concerning it there are two opinions. The first: it is al-Sham and Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), said by Qatadah.

The second: it is Egypt and al-Sham, said by al-Dahhak.

Concerning His saying ﴿a good settlement (mubawwa’ sidq)﴾ there are two interpretations. The first: it is like truthfulness in excellence (al-sidq fi al-fadl).

The second: He gave it to them as charity (tasaddaqa bihi alayhim).

(p-450) It may also bear a third interpretation: He promised it to them, so His promise was a true promise (wa‘d sidq).

﴿And We provided them with good things⦗al-tayyibat⦘﴾, meaning: We made lawful for them the good bounties.

﴿So they did not differ until knowledge came to them﴾, meaning: the Children of Israel did not differ about the fact that Muhammad is a prophet.

﴿Until knowledge came to them⦗hatta ja'ahumu al-'ilm⦘﴾. Concerning it there are two aspects. The first: until Muhammad ﷺ came to them, the one whom they knew to be a prophet; its implied sense is "until the known one came to them." This was said by Ibn Bahr and Ibn Jarir al-Tabari.

The second: until the Qur'an came to them, said by Ibn Zayd.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 10, verses 94–97:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying: ﴿So if you are in doubt about what We have sent down to you﴾. This is an address from Allah to His Prophet. He says: If you, O Muhammad, are in doubt about what We have sent down to you. There are two interpretations of this:

One: that you are in doubt that you are a Messenger.

The second: that you are in doubt that you are written about among them in the Torah and the Gospel.

﴿Then ask those who have been reading the Book before you﴾. Regarding this there are two interpretations:

One: that it means those among them such as ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam and Kaʿb al-Ahbar. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

The second: that it refers to the truthful and God-fearing among them. This was said by al-Dahhak.

If it is asked: Was the Prophet ﷺ ever in doubt? It is said: It has been narrated from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "I do not doubt, and I do not ask." (p-451) As for the meaning of the speech, there are two interpretations: One: that it is an address to the Prophet ﷺ but its intended meaning is others from his community, as the Exalted said: ﴿O Prophet, when you divorce women﴾ [al-Talaq: 1] to the end of the verse. The second: that it is an address that came according to the habit of the Arabs in arousing acceptance and drawing attention to the causes of obedience.

Like the saying of a man to his son: "If you are my son, then be dutiful to me," and to his slave: "If you are my slave, then obey my command." That does not indicate that the son doubts that he is his father's son, nor that the slave doubts that he is the property of his master.

﴿So do not be among the doubters﴾, i.e., among those who doubt.

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying: ﴿Indeed, those upon whom the word of your Lord has been justified will not believe﴾. It admits two interpretations: One: Indeed, those upon whom the word of your Lord has become binding with the threat and anger will never believe.

The second: Indeed, those upon whom His word has fallen by the descent of punishment upon them will never believe.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 10, verse 98:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Why was there not a town that believed so that its faith would benefit it?﴾ The meaning of "town" here is the people of the town.

﴿Except the people of Yunus﴾. They were the people of Nineveh (Naynawa) in the lands of Mosul. Yunus (peace be upon him) had promised them punishment after three days. They said: "Watch Yunus. If he leaves us, then his warning is true." When he left them, they became certain of it, so they turned in fear to an elder among them, who said: "Repent, supplicate, and say: O Living when there is no living, O Living who gives life to the dead, O Living, there is no god but You." So they put on woolen garments, separated every mother from her child, and went out of their town repentant and supplicating. Then God removed the punishment from them, as He, Exalted, said: ﴿We removed from them the punishment of disgrace in the life of this world﴾. On this there are two aspects.

The first: they repented before they saw the punishment, which is why their repentance was accepted. Had they seen it, He would not have accepted it, just as He did not accept the faith of Pharaoh when drowning overtook him.

The second: He, Exalted, specifically granted them the acceptance of repentance after seeing the punishment. Qatadah said: He removed the punishment from them after it had hung over them, and there was between them and the punishment only an inclination (of distance).

﴿And We gave them enjoyment for a time﴾. On this there are two interpretations. The first: until their term (ajal), said by al-Suddi.

The second: until He brings them to Paradise or Hell, said by Ibn 'Abbas.

It is related from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "Caution does not avert decree, but supplication does avert decree." This is because Allah, Exalted, says: ﴿Except the people of Yunus; when they believed, We removed from them the punishment of disgrace﴾. 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, said: that was the day of 'Ashura'.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 10, verses 99–103:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And it is not for a soul to believe except by the permission of Allah﴾. Concerning this there are three interpretations. The first: its meaning is "except by the command of Allah, exalted is He." This was said by al-Hasan.

The second: except by the help of Allah.

The third: except by Allah informing [them] of the paths of guidance and misguidance.

﴿And He places the abomination (ar-rijs) upon those who do not reason﴾. Concerning this there are five interpretations. The first: that ar-rijs is wrath (al-sukhṭ). This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: that it is punishment (al-ʿadhab). This was said by al-Farra'.

The third: that it is sin (al-ithm). This was said by Saʿid ibn Jubayr.

The fourth: that it is that which has no good in it. This was said by Mujahid.

The fifth: that it is Satan (al-shaytan). This was said by Qatadah.

(p. 453) His saying: ﴿upon those who do not reason﴾ means: they do not reason about the command and prohibition of Allah, exalted is He. It is also possible that they are those who do not take heed from His proofs and signs.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 10, verses 104–107:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿And that you should set your face toward the religion, inclining to truth (ḥanīfan)﴾. That is: keep your face turned firmly toward what you have been commanded of the religion, as a ḥanīf. It was also said that by "face" He meant the self.

As for ﴿ḥanīfan﴾, it has six interpretations:

The first: meaning "performing ḥajj," said by Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḥasan, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, ʿAṭiyyah and al-Suddī.

The second: "following" (muttabaʿan), said by Mujāhid.

The third: "upright" (mustaqīman), said by Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb.

The fourth: "sincere" (mukhlisan), said by ʿAṭāʾ.

The fifth: "believing in all the messengers," said by Abū Qilābah. Ḥamzah ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib said:

I praised God when He guided my heart
away from associating partners, to the upright religion (al-dīn al-ḥanīf).

The sixth: "hastening to obedience," derived from al-ḥanaf in the legs, which is when one of them precedes the other.

His saying, may He be exalted and majestic: ﴿Say, "O mankind, the truth has come to you from your Lord."﴾ In it there are two interpretations. The first: it is the Qur'an.
